articles.text: A woman named Dudley came near doing the Irish cause more good yesterday than anything that has happened to it. She shot at O'Donovan Rossa five times, only one shot taking effect, however. We learn with regret that he is liable to get well. He has done nothing but harm to the Irish, and his death is "a consummation devoutly to be wished."
articles.summary: A Mrs. Dudley shot O'Donovan Rossa; the Cow Boy regrets he will recover.

articles.text: With this issue we enter upon Vol. 2, No. 1, of the Cow Boy. We have seen and now see many ways in which the Cow Boy could be improved, and our patrons can be sure that the improvements will occur as soon as our receipts warrant it. We are thankful for all patronage of the last year, and have every confidence that it will be increased in the year to come.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy begins Volume 2, No. 1 and thanks its patrons.

articles.text: Still another illustration of the advantage of advertising for strayed stock in the Cow Boy has come to our notice. The two ponies taken up and advertised by Frank Walker have found an owner in Red Water, Montana. This makes a total of fourteen horses recovered by advertising in the Cow Boy and these owners at least are thorough converts to the benifits thus derived.
articles.summary: Frank Walker's advertised stray ponies found their owner in Red Water, Montana; fourteen horses recovered through Cow Boy ads.

articles.text: A lesson that our stockmen have been slow to learn has been taught them very conclusively this winter. This lesson is to leave yearlings alone. Were it not for the loss on these, especially on Texas yearlings, the loss this winter would have to be measured by fractions. The B X B and V V V outfits seem to have been the heaviest losers and their loss is almost entirely among this class of cattle.
articles.summary: Winter losses fell mostly on yearlings, with the B X B and V V V outfits the heaviest losers.

articles.text: Taking into consideration the rumors of losses from starvation and cold that have been industriously circulated in the east, it may seem almost beyond belief to state the facts. The real facts are that three out of five of all cattle in the Bad Lands, pilgrims included, are now in prime condition for slaughtering. It would be well for any one who doubts this statement to get a horse and ride among the cattle to see for himself. E. G. Paddock, who is certainly a good judge of stock, came in from a ride Saturday and made the statement that he had seen a thousand head of cattle and not a poor one in the lot. Also that he had not seen a dead one. This statement only confirms many others of the same kind that we have repeatedly heard.
articles.summary: Three in five Bad Lands cattle are fit for slaughter; E. G. Paddock saw a thousand head and no poor or dead ones.

articles.text: The lease of the Crow Indian reservation is liable to be nipped in the bud. The investigating committee will report to congress that the Indians who did sign it, about one hundred and forty in all, were frightened into it by threats of agent Armstrong that unless they consented, rations would be stopped April 1. None of the Crows want their reservation used for pasture, and say they will kill all cattle and men found on it. This was a gigantic swindle from beginning to end in the interest of Colorado cattle men, and it is a matter for rejoicing that the plan has been exposed. Dawes, of Massachusetts, the fast friend of the Indian, is on the congressional committee before which the case will come, and it is a certainty that it will not pass congress. Monster petitions are now being signed in Montana against the opening of the reservation.
articles.summary: The Crow reservation lease is expected to fail after charges that agent Armstrong coerced signers.

articles.text: We are glad to see that nearly every paper on the line is agreeing with the Cow Boy in our opposition to the herd law. The opinion is unanimous that we in the Bad Lands, are entitled to a repeal of the herd law and an establishment of a fence law. The most of the papers also agree that it might be better to let the question of applying the fence law to the west Missouri slope outside of the Bad Lands "work out its own salvation." In the present condition of affairs it might be a hardship to compel small farmers in agricultural territory to fence, but as the absolute necessity of diversified farming forces itself on settlers, the herd law will be repealed almost unanimously. It will be no hardship to establish the fence law in the Bad Lands and will keep stockmen from being cinched by evil-minded ranchmen, a danger to which they are now constantly exposed.
articles.summary: Papers along the line agree with the Cow Boy that the Bad Lands should have the herd law repealed and a fence law established.

articles.text: A bill has been introduced into the house to establish a fence law for several counties on the western boundary of Dakota and a consequent repeal of the herd law. The bill includes Villard and Billings counties. It was yesterday referred to the committee on agriculture, where it is liable to lie for some time unless energetic action is taken to have it passed. It will be well to call a special meeting immediately of our cattle association to see that proper arguments are brought to bear for the passage of the bill. During our recent visit in Bismarck a number of legislature's promised their active co-operation in getting a fence law passed for the Bad Lands and we have no doubt of its passing should it receive the unbiased attention of the Legislature. We do not know that the bill has any enemies and certainly did not meet any in Bismarck. The most of the work is done in committees, however, and it may readily happen that evidence against a fence law on general principles may be introduced and our side be wholly unrepresented. "Now is the accepted time" for the stockmen's side to be heard.
articles.summary: A house bill for a fence law covering Villard and Billings counties was referred to committee; the Cow Boy urges a cattle association meeting.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Chinook.
articles.text:
To thee, sweet harbinger of spring days;
To thee, fit thought for poets' lays;
To thee, warmed by Sol's tropic rays;
To thee I lift my voice in praise,
Chinook!

Freed from us now the grip of frost;
The snow and ice are river-tossed
Since thou the hills of the Bad Lands cross'd,
Chinook!

Full many a wind has long been waited,
By ships upon the sea belated,
But thou the wish of stockmen sated,
Chinook!

And as the stockman counts his gold,
And figures cattle bought and sold,
He should to thee his praise unfold,
Chinook!
articles.summary: Poem "Chinook" under Stock Notes, praising the warm wind that freed the Bad Lands from frost.

articles.text: The price of mixed herds, one's and two's from Minnesota and Iowa is now but little if any more than $16 per head landed in Medora. The hard times has especially had its effect on small farmers and as almost all of these have a few head of stock, they are anxious to sell for almost any price.
articles.summary: Mixed herds from Minnesota and Iowa now sell at about $16 a head landed in Medora.

articles.text: The condition of cattle in the Bad Lands is almost beyond the belief of an eastern cattle raiser. They are mostly states' cattle, brought in here, turned loose and never received a grain of any kind. Their entire food is the rich grass and to-day, after enduring the hardest winter and deepest snows on record, a large majority of them are fit for slaughter.
articles.summary: Most Bad Lands cattle, fed only on grass, are fit for slaughter after a hard winter.

articles.text: We see and hear considerable about the letter sent from Fort Keogh to the Pioneer Press, stating that the loss on pilgrims in Montana and Dakota would be fifty to seventy-five per cent. In several instances we have heard that Lieut. J. M. T. Partello was the writer of the letter. We are in a position to know that the Lieutenant's estimate was in no case higher than fifteen per cent. and he averaged it at five to ten. Some other person must have been the author of the canard
articles.summary: The Cow Boy says Lieut. J. M. T. Partello did not write the Fort Keogh letter predicting 50-75 per cent losses.

articles.text: The following is an illustration of making money easily and rapidly. Last June, Lloyd Roberts delivered a bunch of pilgrim one's and two's to Howard Eaton. These were all branded and the most of them taken to Howard's Beaver Creek ranch. There were several strays however, that Howard had never seen after branding and were consequently of no expense whatever. One of these Lloyd bought back last Saturday for $40, butchered at the Co's. slaughter house and made a satisfactory profit on the carcase. The animal dressed nearly six hundred pounds and was literally covered with fat and in perfect condition for butchering, although it would have increased proportionalety in value had it been allowed to live till it was a three or four year old. As this steer was brought in the latter part of last June and sold the last of January, it will be seen that Howard's profit was 313 per cent. This profit was net, as there was not a solitary cent spent on this steer after branding. Of course this is an exceptional case but it is one that can be almost duplicated wholesale by any one driving in a large herd of cattle here and being ready at any time to sell fat cattle. The local trade here and up and down the line would alone make it profitable, and by this means the refrigerator company could be kept running eight or nine months in the year and they would doubtless purchase all fat cattle that could be brought in.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts bought back a stray pilgrim steer from Howard Eaton's herd for $40 and butchered it, showing a 313 per cent profit.

articles.text: Dr J. J. Clemmer, of Cresco, Iowa, and partner in the Cave Hills cattle ranch of Clemmer & Dell, is another convert to our Polled-Angus list. He intends materially increasing his herd and will use Polled-Angus bulls exclusively. The merits of polled cattle have been a long time forcing themselves on the attention of the public, but it is only a matter of time when all will become converts.
articles.summary: Dr. J. J. Clemmer of the Cave Hills ranch of Clemmer & Dell will use Polled-Angus bulls exclusively.

articles.text: Buyers are said by a correspondent to be in Texas in large numbers and there will be no difficulty in selling, provided the sellers will take all risk of contagion. This they are not willing to do and we doubt if any cattle have been sold except to be received at the option of the buyer. This is the animus of Texas favoring a national trail. In other words, they want original or second buyers to shoulder the responsibility that belongs to them.
articles.summary: Texas sellers will not take the risk of contagion, which explains Texas support for a national trail.

articles.text: A point that we have before alluded to and one that must at some times occupy the attention of congress, seems now more worthy of consideration than ever. It is the German method of dealing with contagious diseases. A proper number of inspectors is appointed, before one of whom every case of contagious disease must be brought. If the disease is incurable, the animal is immediately killed and two-thirds of its value returned by the government to the owner. It will be seen that this plan is just, as the spread of the disease might be a national calamity, and thus the people at large would bear part of the burden. The amount returned to the owner is no more than two-thirds, so that there can be no gain to him by having the animal killed. This system, with a few modifications, would work to a charm in the United States. It would be a little difficult in the case of large herds, but as prompt action would be the most important in these cases, means could be found to bring the attention of the authorities to them and stamp out almost any disease in its infancy. Until some such action as this is taken, it will be utterly impossible to deal with the periodical scares of foot-and-mouth disease, pleuro-pneumonia, Texas fever, etc.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy recommends the German system of inspecting and indemnifying diseased cattle.

articles.text: Dr. J. H. Detmer, of the agricultural department at Washington, has submitted his report on Texas fever to commissioner Loring The doctor certainly advances some original views on the subject, which in substance are as follows: The half-dead grass of Texas pastures becomes infected with a kind of bacteria, which cause all the symptoms of Texas fever. The disease is spread by the Texans already infected by eating the grass, being driven north and grazing over lands which are afterwards used by northern cattle. The bacteria are swarming in the blood, meat and secretions of the Texans, and the saliva makes the bacteria cling to the blades of grass, ready to spread the disease to any northern cattle which may graze over the same ground. When lodged on the grass, the bacteria germinate and are then more deadly than ever. It is well known that northern cattle grazing after a Texas herd, are not immediately smitten with the disease, while those grazing after a lapse of several weeks are almost immediately stricken. Dr. Detmer's germination theory explains this exactly. The reason that Texas cattle do not themselves suffer with the disease, is that they are from their birth inoculated against it by being born with bacteria in their systems. The doctor's theory altogether is very interesting, explains fully all the phenomena of the disease, and is the most satisfactory explanation yet given.
articles.summary: Summary of Dr. J. H. Detmer's bacteria theory of Texas fever, submitted to Commissioner Loring.

articles.headline: The Texas Trail.
articles.text:
The discussion on the Texas cattle trail is becoming warmer, and from reliable sources we learn that there is imminent danger of bloodshed between its defenders and opponents. As some may not know the extent of territory asked for, we will state that Texas cattlemen want a trail six miles wide from some point in Texas to Canada, and that at convenient points the trail shall be widened sufficiently to allow for pasturage, and if found necessary, quarantine grounds. To say the least, the request is not conspicuous for its modesty. As "Griff," of Bismarck says, "They want the whole world—and some of the outside." In return for this trail, the Texas cattlemen are willing to allow the rich grasses of Montana and Dakota to fatten their stock, and use the profits thus gained to build up some other portion of the country. To begin with, there is no likelihood of congress granting the trail asked for, but if it should, it could easily be made inoperative by the different states through which it runs, passing rigid quarantine laws for their own protection. The fact of the matter is that the trail would scarcely be in operation before Texas fever would fasten its deadly grip on a large majority of all cattle here and between here and Texas.

There will be no hardship to Texas cattle owners by a refusal to establish a trail that they have not brought on themselves. Of course, it is harder to sell cattle from Texas than it is from Dakota or Montana, but is that any reason why our stockmen should suffer that outside men may reap a profit? Would it not be as just that the gold mines of of Butte should suffer because the Black Hills gold product is harder to get to a market?

If the Texas cattle men are so hard up for a market or for pasturage, they should sell out in Texas and go to places where both are handy, and not attempt to bring loss to our cattlemen. We prophesy that the Texas cattle trail as proposed will never be in operation.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy opposes the proposed six-mile-wide national Texas cattle trail and predicts it will never operate.

articles.text: Windy Bill, Dutch Bill and Jay Gould are now well on their way to South America, where they will teach the pilgrims how to "run stage wagons."
articles.summary: Windy Bill, Dutch Bill and Jay Gould are bound for South America to run stage wagons.

articles.text: A letter from Russ Wilson, foreman of the E 6, states that the loss there will be small, and that the winter evenings are spent in eating hickory nuts and big red apples. We're coming, Russ.
articles.summary: Russ Wilson, E 6 foreman, writes that losses there will be small.

articles.text: B. Barr is still in Kansas City, and will go to Texas to purchase cattle as soon as the present complications are settled. He does not look for an amicable settlement of the difficulties, nor a very speedy one.
articles.summary: B. Barr, in Kansas City, will buy Texas cattle once the present difficulties are settled.

articles.text: Wm. Van Driesche, the treasurer of the school board, states that a number who subscribed have not paid. In such a movement as this, there should be no hanging back. Bills must be paid and it is to the interest of every one that they be paid promptly.
articles.summary: School board treasurer Wm. Van Driesche says some subscribers have not paid.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper is at his home in Binghamton, N. Y. Provided there is no difficulty in getting cattle out of Texas, he will drive a herd into the Bad Lands. If the difficulty is not settled, he will put off the drive another year and go into some business with St. Paul as his headquarters.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper, at Binghamton, N. Y., will drive a herd to the Bad Lands if Texas cattle can be moved.

articles.text: Work on the Hotel de Mores will begin almost immediately. All the partitions will be taken out and changed, the whole building plastered and calcimined, a porch built on the west and south sides, an addition built and as soon as the weather permits the whole building will be veneered.
articles.summary: Remodeling of the Hotel de Mores is to begin almost immediately.

articles.summary: Arrivals and departures on the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.'s line since the last issue.

articles.text: At no distant day there will be a shooting match here for a friendly trial of skill. The contest is open to all, each to use any gun he pleases. Preliminaries can be arranged on the ground. Each contestant will put a dollar in a general purse, to be taken by the winner. A six-shooter contest may also be arranged.
articles.summary: A shooting match, open to all with a dollar entry, will be held soon.

articles.text: One of our aspiring Nimrods thought he would make a mash on a dining car steward and give him a doe's head, that he explained he would not part with to any one else, as it was not only the first deer he had ever killed, but one of the prettiest heads he had ever seen. As the steward was receiving it, Dan walked up and said: "Hello, Max, what are you doing with my deer head?" Explanations.
articles.summary: Anecdote: a local hunter's gift of a deer head to a dining car steward is exposed by Dan as his own trophy.

articles.text: As we enter upon the second volume of the Cow Boy, we hope that all our subscribers, especially our local ones, will make an effort toward extending our circulation. There is not a solitary one of our subscribers that cannot induce one or more other persons to subscribe. It is well worth the trial, and our friends will be surprised at the good they can accomplish by a little effort. Try it and see.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy asks subscribers to help extend its circulation as it enters its second volume.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a letter from Vic. Smith, written from Chicago, in which he gives a vivid description of his travels so far. Happening into a shooting gallery in Milwaukee he "gave a specimen of western marksmanship," and was immediately offered a salary of $40 per week. He says "Medora is good enough" for him, and will return. He had with him Bob Robert's buckskin suit, and took first prize at a masquerade. As he stepped off the cars in Chicago, one man was engaging in the festive operation of shooting another. He did a good job, and as Vic says, "as clean as I ever saw it done in the west." Vic's father and brother are very sick, and this, coupled with bad reports of the New Orleans exposition he heard from friends, has decided him to give up his trip there. He intends returning about February 25.
articles.summary: Vic Smith writes from Chicago of shooting-gallery fame and a masquerade prize; he gives up the New Orleans trip and expects to return about February 25.

articles.headline: SMILES.
articles.text:
O when the maiden plays me false,
And loves the other fellow,
For maiden's scorn, and the heart forlorn
My solace is tobacco.

Philosophy doth comfort me
With counsel sage and mellow,
When that I stifle dreams of wife
And all that, in tobacco.

For when I whiff the ringlets up,
And watch them, hazy, yellow,
Her features there, with the wavy hair,
Repent me of tobacco.

But when the ringlets fade in air
And the vision fair dispel,—O,
No falser shade than the living maid,
I reason, in tobacco.

And so I whiff and smoke in peace,
A well contented fellow,
The heart forlorn and the maiden's scorn
Forgotten in tobacco.

—[Amherst Student.

A man we heard of is so short that when he is ill he don't know whether he has headache or corns.—[Chicago Sun.

"My dear, look below," said a Harlem man, just as he stood on the bridge with his wife and gazed at a tug hauling a line of barges. "Such is life—the tug is like a man working and toiling, while the barge, like women, are"— "I know," interrupted Mrs. G., acridly, "the tug does the blowing and the barges bear the burdens."—[Ex.

"I have the honor," said General Butler, "of knowing three of the greatest living liars in America." "Who are they?" asked the venerable Sam Ward, as he dropped a chicken partridge to listen to the general. "Well, sir," said the general, with his customary thoughtful scratch of his head, "Mark Twain is one and Eli Perkins is the other two."—[Ex. All which goes to show that General Butler and Alaska John are not on terms of intimacy.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press advertised for a boy at two dollars a week, and received 250 answers. There seems to have been a sort of competitive examination or adoption of civil service rules in selecting a boy, and the one who wrote the following letter was selected: "Mister P., Pioneer Press: I want the Job my fokses is not rich & I hev got to russell. They are ded. It betes hel how hard times is I am 14 & kin do chores I look good with new clothes on I would like to get a good place in your offis I kin learn fast.—[Chicago Tribune.

To the young the future has a roseate hue. The roseate hue comes high, but we have to use it in this place. To the young there spread out a glorious range of possibilities. After the youth has indorsed for an intimate friend a few times, and purchased the paper at the bank later on, the horizon won't seem to horizon so tumultuously as it did aforetime. I remember at one time of purchasing such a piece of accommodation paper at a bank, and I still have it. I didn't need it any more than a cat needs 11 tails at one and the same time. Still the bank made it an object to me, and I secured it. Such things as these harshly knock the fluff and bloom off the cheek of youth, and prompt us to turn the strawberry-box bottom side up before we purchase it. Youth is gay and hopeful, age is covered with experience and scars where the skin has been knocked off and had to grow on again. To the young a dollar looks large and strong, but to the middle-aged and the old it is weak and inefficient. When we are in the heyday and fizz of existence, we believe everything, but after awhile we murmur, "What's that you're givin' us," or words of a like character. Age brings caution and a lot of shop-worn experience purchased at the highest market price. Time brings vain regrets and wisdom teeth that can be left in a glass of water over night.[—Bill Nye.
articles.summary: Column of clipped humor (tobacco poem from the Amherst Student, jokes, Pioneer Press office-boy letter, Bill Nye) with a local quip about Alaska John.
